Question two. Why favor composition over inheritance? Inheritance ties a subclass to its parent's implementation, so a change upstream can break it. That's the fragile base class problem. The shop's loyalty program extends the shopping cart, and counts each item as it's added. The cart's add-all adds them one at a time, so three items count three. Then the cart team speeds add-all up, and it stops adding them one at a time. The count for those three drops to zero, and nobody touched the loyalty code. Composition holds a cart and delegates to it, counting in its own methods. It relies only on what the cart promises: three before the change, three after. It also combines freely. Notifications go by email, text or push, at one of three timings. A subclass per pair is nine, and a fourth channel makes twelve. Composition gives each notifier one channel and one timing: six parts, then seven. A customer who switches to the daily digest swaps one part, at runtime. Keep inheritance for a genuine subtype. Which raises what makes one genuine.

Question three. What is the Liskov substitution principle, in plain terms? A subclass must be usable anywhere its parent is expected, without surprising the caller. The classic trap is a square that subclasses a rectangle. It keeps its sides equal, so setting its width sets its height too. Code written for rectangles sets the width to five, then the height to four, and expects an area of twenty. Hand it a square, and it gets sixteen. So a subclass mustn't demand more of its callers, or promise them less. And the fix isn't a cleverer square. Don't make a square a kind of resizable rectangle: shapes that can't be resized, or two siblings that each work out their own area, both keep every promise.
